title: Internal Trade
summary: Internal trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within the geographical boundaries of a country (also called domestic or home trade). Features: it takes place within the home country; payment is made in the home currency; it involves producers, consumers and middlemen; it consists of a distribution network of middlemen and agencies. On the basis of volume of goods traded it is classified as wholesale trade and retail trade.

Wholesale trade is buying goods in large quantities from producers and selling to other traders in smaller quantities. Wholesalers perform bulk buying and bulk breaking. Functions: procurement of goods, grading and packing, transporting, warehousing, financing (to manufacturers and retailers), risk bearing, providing market information and selling. Services to manufacturers: bulk buying and warehousing facility. Services to retailers: regular supply, financial help (credit), advertisement, market information and risk protection.

Retail trade is buying goods from manufacturers or wholesalers and selling them to final consumers in small quantities. Characteristics: deals in a variety of items; buys in bulk and sells in small quantities; located near main markets; buys on credit and sells for cash; indirect relation with the manufacturer but direct link with consumers. Services to consumers: regular supply, convenient location, wide choice, home delivery and consumer education; to wholesalers: market information, help in distribution, large-scale production and selling new products.

Middlemen (wholesalers and retailers) free the producer from transport, warehousing, financing and marketing, and make goods available at convenient times and places; but they add to the price (e.g. a pen costing Rs 5 sold for Rs 8.50: middlemen's margin Rs 3.50), may hoard or adulterate and may delay goods; their benefits outweigh the problems.

Wholesale versus retail: a few items versus a variety; large quantities versus small; buys from manufacturers versus from wholesalers; sells to retailers versus to consumers; large capital versus small; direct link with producers versus direct link with consumers; located with other wholesalers versus near residential areas; no elaborate display versus attractive display.

Retail business is classified by whether there is a fixed place of business: itinerant retailing (hawkers, peddlers, cart vendors, weekly bazaars or haats, door-to-door sale; bargaining and unbranded goods) and fixed shop retailing (small scale and large scale).

Small-scale fixed shops: general store (variety of daily-use goods), single line store (one line, e.g. bookshop, medicine shop), speciality store (products of a particular brand, e.g. Woodland) and second-hand goods shop.

Large-scale retail: Departmental store: a large store selling a wide variety of goods in one building divided into departments, under central management, with facilities like home delivery and credit, in the main commercial centres (merits: all goods under one roof, economies of large purchase, efficient staff, one department advertises the others; limitations: large capital, far from residences, high operating cost, no personal contact). Multiple shops (chain stores): shops with the same name and decoration owned by big manufacturers selling the same goods at uniform price (Raymonds, McDonald's, Domino's); merits: easy to recognise, eliminate middlemen, economies, cheaper, standard goods; limitations: limited variety, only cash, no bargaining, branch managers lack initiative. Supermarket: a large self-service store selling food and household goods at reasonable prices; no home delivery, credit or salespersons; merits: wide range, standard quality, cheaper, low operating cost; limitations: large capital, cash only, not suitable for goods needing salesmen. Consumer cooperative store: owned by a cooperative society of consumers; goods at lower prices, cash sales, near residential areas, profit distributed as bonus; limitations: inadequate funds, limited growth, lack of professional managers. Mail order retailing: orders are placed by post in response to advertisements, catalogues and brochures; goods dispatched by post or courier. Franchise: the franchisor allows the franchisee to use its brand name, products and business system in return for a fee or royalty (e.g. fast-food chains).

objective: Match: (i) Bulk Breaking (ii) Bulk Buying with (a) Wholesaler (b) Retailer.
(i) Bulk breaking – (b) Retailer (buys in bulk and sells in small quantities); (ii) bulk buying – (a) Wholesaler.

Fill in the blank: ______ refers to buying goods from the manufacturers or wholesalers and selling them to final consumers.
Retail trade.

Give two characteristics of internal trade.
Buying and selling take place within the home country; payment is in the home country's currency.

Write WT for wholesale trade and RT for retail trade: (a) dealing in limited variety; (b) buying goods from wholesalers for resale; (c) grading and packaging; (d) located near residential areas.
(a) WT. (b) RT. (c) WT. (d) RT.
Identify the type of retailing: (a) A store dealing in books. (b) A store with all varieties of one brand. (c) Selling goods on the pavement.
(a) Single line store. (b) Speciality store. (c) Itinerant retailing (hawkers).
Name any three types of large-scale retail trade.
Departmental store, multiple shops and supermarket (also consumer cooperative store, mail order and franchise).

(a) A wholesaler has a direct link with producers. (b) The capital required is large in wholesale trade.

(i) False. (ii) True.
vsa: Explain why intermediaries are used despite adding to cost.
They increase the efficiency of distribution by bulk breaking, storing, financing and making goods available to consumers near them.
State any two features of internal trade.
Trade within the geographical boundaries of a country and payment in the home currency.
Small-scale retail trade in which retailers move around and sell goods directly to consumers without a fixed shop.
What is a franchise form of retail trade? State any one feature.
A franchisor permits the franchisee to use its brand name and business system for a fee; the franchisee owns and runs the outlet under the franchisor's guidelines.
Who owns (a) a departmental store (b) multiple shops?
(a) A company or business house. (b) Big manufacturers.
State any two merits of supermarkets.
A wide range of daily-use goods under one roof and lower prices due to bulk purchase and avoiding middlemen.
sa: What is a departmental store? Give any three features.

A large retail store selling a wide variety of goods in one building divided into departments under central management; each department sells specific goods; it provides facilities like home delivery and credit.
What are consumer cooperative stores? State their merits.
Retail stores owned by cooperative societies of consumers. Merits: low prices (no middlemen), cash sales so no bad debts and profit distributed to members as bonus.
What is a franchise form of retail trade? State any three features.
A franchisor allows the franchisee to use its brand and system. Features: the franchisee uses the brand name, pays a fee or royalty and follows the franchisor's standards.
Explain any three services provided by retailers to consumers.
Regular supply, convenient location and wide choice (also home delivery and consumer education).
State any three limitations of multiple shops.
Limited variety, only cash sales and no bargaining.
Explain any three merits of departmental stores.
Goods under one roof, economies of large purchase and efficient staff.
la: Define a wholesaler and identify any four functions performed by them.

A wholesaler buys goods in bulk from manufacturers and sells to retailers. Functions: procurement of goods, grading and packing, transporting, warehousing, financing, risk bearing, market information and selling.
Distinguish between wholesale trade and retail trade.
Items, quantity, source, customers, capital, relationship and display differ: wholesale deals in a few items in bulk with large capital; retail deals in a variety in small quantities near consumers.
Explain the types of large-scale retail trade.
Departmental stores, multiple shops, supermarkets, consumer cooperative stores, mail order and franchise, each with features and merits.
Explain the merits and limitations of supermarkets.
Merits: wide range, standard quality, cheaper goods and low operating cost; limitations: large capital, cash only and self-service limits suitable goods.
Explain the role of middlemen in the chain of distribution.
Wholesalers save the producer's effort, provide credit and information; retailers supply goods to consumers, offer services and feedback; but they add to price.
